title: Hilbert's 18th Problem: The Kepler Conjecture
content: The module docstring introduces the Kepler Conjecture as part of Hilbert's 18th Problem. The FCC lattice achieves density π/(3√2) ≈ 74.05%, proven by Hales (1998) with a computer-assisted proof spanning 250+ pages and 40,000+ lines of code, formally verified by the Flyspeck project in HOL Light (2014). The file covers the 2D case (hexagonal packing, Thue 1892), the 3D case (FCC, Hales 1998), kissing numbers, and higher-dimensional results including Viazovska's Fields Medal work on dimensions 8 and 24.
mathContext: The Kepler Conjecture states: $\sup\{\delta(P) : P \text{ is a sphere packing in } \mathbb{R}^3\} = \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.74048$. This supremum is achieved by the FCC lattice and the HCP (hexagonal close-packed) arrangement, both of which are stackings of hexagonal layers.

title: Packing Density Definitions
content: Defines sphereVolume r = (4/3)πr³ and diskArea r = πr². The PackingDensity structure wraps a real number with proofs that 0 ≤ density ≤ 1. For lattice packings, density = (volume of one sphere) / (volume of fundamental domain). This gives a clean abstraction for comparing packing densities across dimensions.
mathContext: The packing density $\delta$ of an arrangement is $\delta = \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{\text{Vol}(\text{spheres} \cap B_R)}{\text{Vol}(B_R)}$. For a lattice packing with fundamental domain $\mathcal{F}$: $\delta = \frac{V_n r^n}{\text{Vol}(\mathcal{F})}$ where $V_n = \frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2+1)}$ is the unit ball volume.

title: Thue's Theorem: 2D Optimal Packing
content: The hexagonal packing density π/(2√3) ≈ 90.69% is defined and proven positive (hexagonalDensity2D_pos). Thue's theorem (axiomatized) states this is optimal among all disk packings in ℝ². The kissing number in 2D is 6. The proof proceeds by showing every Voronoi cell of a non-overlapping disk packing has area ≥ 2√3r², with equality iff the cell is a regular hexagon. Fejes Tóth (1940) provided the first fully rigorous proof.
mathContext: For the hexagonal lattice: fundamental domain area $= 2\sqrt{3}r^2$ (rhombus with angles $60°$ and $120°$), disk area $= \pi r^2$, giving $\delta_{\text{hex}} = \frac{\pi r^2}{2\sqrt{3}r^2} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.9069$. The Voronoi cell argument: for any packing of disks of radius $r$, the Voronoi cell around each center has area $\geq 2\sqrt{3}r^2$.

title: Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) Lattice
content: The FCC density π/(3√2) ≈ 0.7405 is defined, proven positive, and shown to lie in (0.74, 0.75) via axiomatized numerical bounds. An alternative representation π√2/6 is given with axiomatized equivalence. The kissing number in 3D is 12 (Schütte-van der Waerden, 1953). The FCC lattice places sphere centers at cube corners and face centers; equivalently, it is a stacking of hexagonal layers in ABCABC pattern (vs ABAB for HCP, which has the same density).
mathContext: FCC lattice vectors: $\mathbf{a}_1 = \frac{a}{2}(0,1,1)$, $\mathbf{a}_2 = \frac{a}{2}(1,0,1)$, $\mathbf{a}_3 = \frac{a}{2}(1,1,0)$ with lattice constant $a$. Sphere radius $r = \frac{a\sqrt{2}}{4}$. Fundamental domain volume $= \frac{a^3}{4} = 4\sqrt{2}r^3$. Density $= \frac{(4/3)\pi r^3}{4\sqrt{2}r^3} = \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}}$.

title: The Kepler Conjecture (Hales 1998)
content: The main theorem: no packing of congruent spheres in ℝ³ has density greater than FCC. Axiomatized as kepler_conjecture : d.density ≤ fccDensity for any PackingDensity. Hales' proof (1998) involved 250+ pages and 40,000+ lines of code, reviewed by 12 referees over 4 years, published in Annals (2005), and formally verified by Flyspeck in HOL Light (2014). Gauss (1831) had earlier proven the weaker result that FCC is optimal among lattice packings only.
mathContext: The Kepler Conjecture: $\forall$ sphere packings $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$: $\delta(P) \leq \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}}$. Hales' proof reduces to a finite optimization problem by showing that the local density around each sphere center can be bounded using a decomposition into Delaunay stars, then verifying ~5000 linear programs computationally.

title: Higher Dimensions: Viazovska's Theorem
content: The E₈ lattice density π⁴/384 ≈ 25.37% is defined and proven positive. Kissing numbers are recorded: k(2) = 6, k(3) = 12, k(8) = 240, k(24) = 196,560. Viazovska's theorem (axiomatized) states that the E₈ lattice achieves maximum density in ℝ⁸, proven using modular forms and the Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound. She won the 2022 Fields Medal. The optimal packing is unknown in dimensions 4-7, 9-23, and ≥25.
mathContext: Viazovska's proof constructs an auxiliary function $f : \mathbb{R}^8 \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying: (1) $f(0) = \hat{f}(0)$, (2) $f(x) \leq 0$ for $|x| \geq 1$, (3) $\hat{f}(t) \geq 0$ for all $t$. Such $f$ certifies optimality via the Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound. The function is built from quasimodular forms for $\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

title: Applications of Sphere Packing
content: Documents four areas of practical impact: (1) error-correcting codes — dense lattice packings correspond to efficient codes, with E₈ and Leech lattices giving exceptional error-correction; (2) crystallography — FCC appears in aluminum, copper, gold, silver, and lead; (3) digital communications — sphere packing bounds (Shannon capacity) limit signal constellation efficiency; (4) computational geometry — mesh generation and molecular simulation.
mathContext: The connection to coding theory: a lattice packing of density $\delta$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ yields an error-correcting code with rate proportional to $\log_2(\delta)$. The E₈ and Leech lattice codes achieve rates close to the Shannon limit in their respective dimensions.

title: Density Decreases with Dimension
content: Two comparison axioms establish hexagonal_gt_fcc (π/(2√3) > π/(3√2)) and fcc_gt_e8 (π/(3√2) > π⁴/384). The first reduces to 3√2 > 2√3, equivalently 18 > 12 by squaring. The theorem density_decreases_with_dimension combines both into a conjunction. This illustrates the 'curse of dimensionality' for packing: higher-dimensional spheres leave more unfilled space.
mathContext: The comparison chain: $\delta_{2D} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.907 > \delta_{3D} = \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.740 > \delta_{8D} = \frac{\pi^4}{384} \approx 0.254$. The proof of $\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}} > \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}}$ reduces to $3\sqrt{2} > 2\sqrt{3}$, i.e., $\sqrt{18} > \sqrt{12}$.

title: Exports and Summary
content: The #check section verifies all major exports: hexagonal and FCC density definitions, Thue's and Kepler's theorems, numerical bounds, and the density comparison chain. The key verified statements are hexagonal_is_optimal_2D, fcc_is_optimal_3D, and density_decreases_with_dimension.
mathContext: The formalization establishes optimality in three dimensions: $\delta_{\text{hex}}$ in 2D (Thue), $\delta_{\text{FCC}}$ in 3D (Hales), $\delta_{E_8}$ in 8D (Viazovska), with the density chain $\delta_{2D} > \delta_{3D} > \delta_{8D}$ proved.
